title: The board it was never shown

chapters.name: Statistics or a world?
chapters.note: never shown a board ... does it have one anyway?

cap.1: A model learns Othello only from lists of moves, never seeing a board. Does it memorise what tends to follow what, or quietly build the board?
cap.2: OthelloGPT: a GPT with a 59-move context, trained on random legal games to predict the next legal move. The question: surface statistics, or a model of the board generating the data?
cap.3: Trained on uniformly random legal sequences, its optimum is uniform over legal next moves, so it must somehow know what is legal. Whether it computes a board to do that is testable.

cap.1: Picture a blindfolded player who has only ever heard moves called out. If they keep a board in their head, two tests will show it: read it, then change it.
cap.2: Test one: probe the residual stream for each square's state. Test two: edit that state mid-forward-pass and see whether the model's legal-move predictions follow the edit.
cap.3: Probing shows the board is decodable; intervention shows the model uses it. Li et al. did both: the cleanest evidence that a next-token predictor models the process generating its data.

chapters.name: Read the board
chapters.title: what the probe reads: blank (·), theirs (T), mine (M)

cap.1: Read the player's mental board one square at a time: blank, theirs, or mine? A small reader trained on the model's insides can do it.
cap.2: A probe per square maps the residual stream to three options: blank, theirs, mine. The transformer stays frozen; only the probe learns, from cached activations and the true board.
cap.3: Probe shape [d_model, row, col, options]. Softmax is translation invariant, so each square has two degrees of freedom: blank − (mine + theirs)/2, and mine − theirs.

props.label: next call: legal for the NEW board

cap.1: Now secretly flip a piece on the player's mental board. If their next call is legal for the new board, even one no real game could reach, the board is in use.
cap.2: Li et al. edited the residual stream by gradient descent through the probe until it read a different board. The model then predicted legal moves for that board, including unreachable ones.
cap.3: The causal edit turns a probing result into a claim about computation. But gradient descent through a two-layer probe can push activations far off-distribution: strong edits are weaker evidence.

chapters.name: The black-and-white wrinkle

left.title: Ask: black or white?
lines: model or probe doing the work?

chapters.verdict: Needing a clever probe hints you asked the wrong question.

cap.1: The first reader had to be clever, which is suspicious: maybe it did the thinking. Asking 'mine or theirs?', not 'black or white?', let a simple one work.
cap.2: Li et al.'s headline was a non-linear world model, since linear probes failed. Nanda's follow-up: the model plays both sides, and in the mine/theirs basis a linear probe reads the board.
cap.3: Odd- and even-move black − white probe directions are near antipodal because the colour label flips each move. An expressive probe can compute a feature from simpler ones, so linear readability matters.

marks.label: gradient descent through an MLP probe

cap.1: A gentle nudge that still changes the player's moves is hard to explain away. Bulldoze their mental board and you may have made a thought they never have.
cap.2: The weaker the intervention, the stronger the evidence. Changing one residual coordinate along mine − theirs after layer 4 flips the legal-move predictions, with no gradient descent.
cap.3: Gradient descent through a two-layer probe can produce off-distribution residual streams; a single-coordinate linear edit yielding coherent legal moves for the new board is hard to explain unless the model uses that direction.

chapters.name: Decodable isn't used
items: Pair every probe with the cheapest causal edit
A readable board becomes a readout for circuits

cap.1: Finding a picture in a model's head isn't enough; show the model acts on it. That test sits under every claim about what AI knows, and every way to steer it.
cap.2: Probe accuracy measures what is decodable, not what the model uses. Follow every probe with a causal edit, and treat a failed linear probe as a hint you picked the wrong labels.
cap.3: By layer 4, about 64 of 512 residual dimensions encode 'my colour' and 60 encode 'blank': a readout for asking what downstream neurons read and write. Decodable versus used carries every probe-based safety argument.

coda.title: Edit the board: tap a square to cycle blank, mine, theirs

readouts.label: legal moves for the player to move
in the model's terms
readouts.f: (sum(G.map(row => sum(row.map(v => v % 3 == 1 ? 1 : 0))))) + ' mine, ' + (sum(G.map(row => sum(row.map(v => v % 3 == 2 ? 1 : 0))))) + ' theirs'

readouts.label: the same pieces in colours
readouts.f: ((m, t) => 'black to play: ' + m + ' black, ' + t + ' white · white to play: ' + t + ' black, ' + m + ' white')(sum(G.map(row => sum(row.map(v => v % 3 == 1 ? 1 : 0)))), sum(G.map(row => sum(row.map(v => v % 3 == 2 ? 1 : 0)))))

caption.1: Tap squares to cycle blank, mine, theirs, and watch the legal moves update: the edit experiment in miniature. Mine and theirs stay put; colours swap each turn.
caption.2: Change the board and the set of legal next moves changes, which is what OthelloGPT's predictions did under the edit. Its code is mine versus theirs, so a piece reads 'black' one move and 'white' the next.
caption.3: Legal: an empty square with a run of theirs capped by mine in any of 8 directions. A black/white label flips sign each ply while mine/theirs does not: the reason odd and even colour probes point opposite ways.

hamming.what: A GPT trained only on legal Othello move sequences, which turns out to build and use an internal board it was never shown.
hamming.when: Whenever you ask whether a model has learned a model of the world or just surface statistics, and want a testbed where the answer is checkable.
hamming.why: It is the cleanest evidence that next-token prediction can produce a world model, and it teaches the probe-then-intervene discipline behind every such claim.

object.title: The board in its head
object.subtitle: The starting position as the model codes it: height is each square's reading along its mine-minus-theirs direction.

knobs.label: edit d4 to read 'mine' (0 off, 1 on)

cap.1: The opening position: two black pieces, two white. Height is how the model reads each square. Black to play, so the black pieces stand tall: they are 'mine'.
cap.2: Bars show each square's projection onto its mine − theirs direction. Blank squares sit flat. Black to move, so black = mine.
cap.3: The per-square mine − theirs probe direction applied to the residual stream; heights are schematic (±1 around a baseline), positions are the true Othello opening.

cap.1: Now it's white's turn. Not one piece changed colour, yet every reading flipped: the black pieces now read as 'theirs'.
cap.2: Same physical board, other player to move: the model's code for every piece changes sign, because it tracks mine versus theirs.
cap.3: The model's board code is relative to the player to move; absolute colour is (mine − theirs) times a parity sign, a product no single linear direction can read.

cap.1: So a reader asking 'black or white?' along one fixed direction is right on black's turns and exactly wrong on white's. No single straight line works.
cap.2: A black/white probe fitted on odd moves points one way, on even moves the opposite way. That is why the linear probe looked like it failed.
cap.3: Odd and even black − white probe directions come out with cosine ≈ −1; averaging them with the right sign recovers the mine direction.

cap.1: The intervention: nudge d4 so it reads 'mine'. The model now predicts legal moves for that edited board.
cap.2: One coordinate changed along d4's mine − theirs direction, after layer 4. The legal-move predictions shift to match the new board.
cap.3: A single-coordinate linear edit is the weakest useful causal test; coherent legal moves for the edited board mean the model reads this direction.

cap.1: From above: the board in the model's own terms. It is the only frame where one straight line reads every square, on every turn.
cap.2: In the mine/theirs basis the representation is linear and stable across moves; that is what made cheap probing and cheap editing possible.
cap.3: About 64 of 512 residual dimensions encode 'my colour' and 60 encode 'blank' (the four centre squares are never blank), giving a readout for circuit analysis.

predict.q: OthelloGPT was never shown a board. After probing and editing it, what do we conclude?

options.t: It computes the board state and uses it to predict legal moves
It only memorises which moves tend to follow which

predict.why: A probe reads the board, and editing it makes the legal-move predictions follow the edit, even for unreachable boards.

predict.q: Why did a linear black/white probe struggle?

options.t: The model codes mine vs theirs, so a piece's code flips sign each move
The board is stored in a genuinely non-linear way

predict.why: Odd- and even-move black − white directions are near opposite. In the mine/theirs basis a linear probe works.

predict.q: Which result is stronger evidence that the model uses a direction?

options.t: A one-coordinate nudge after layer 4 flips the legal moves
Gradient descent through an MLP probe flips the legal moves

predict.why: The weaker the intervention, the less it can push activations off-distribution, so its success says more.

object.where: Any claim that a network 'knows' something: probe it, then nudge it and watch the behaviour follow.
